Swift provides many fundamental data types, including Int for integers, Double  for floating-point values, Bool  for Boolean values,
and String  for text. Swift also provides powerful versions of the three primary collection types, Array , Set, and Dictionary , as
described in Collection Types .
Swift uses variables to store and refer to values by an identifying name. Swift also makes extensive use of variables whose values
can’t be changed. These are known as constants, and are used throughout Swift to make code safer and clearer in intent when
you work with values that don’t need to change.
In addition to familiar types, Swift introduces advanced types such as tuples. Tuples enable you to create and pass around
groupings of values. You can use a tuple to return multiple values from a function as a single compound value.
Swift handles the absence of a value using optional types. Optionals say either “there is a value, which is x” or “there isn’t a value

**Send‑retry behavior in the SDK – v2 vs. v3**

| Aspect | v2 (client_send.md) | v3 (client_send.md) |
|--------|---------------------|---------------------|
| **Default `max_retries`** | **3** retries | **5** retries |
| **Default `retry_backoff_ms`** | **250 ms** base back‑off between attempts | **500 ms** base back‑off between attempts |
| **Default `timeout_ms`** | **30 000 ms** (30 s) total wall‑clock budget for the whole send (including retries) | **15 000 ms** (15 s) total wall‑clock budget (half of v2) |
| **Automatic retry logic** | `Client.send()` automatically retries retry‑able error codes (as indicated in `errors.md`) up to `max_retries`. | Same automatic retry mechanism, but with the higher retry count and longer back‑off. |
| **Rate‑limit handling (`429 RATE_LIMITED`)** | Retries up to `max_retries` with the 250 ms back‑off. | Retries up to `max_retries` with the 500 ms back‑off. |
| **Error raised after exhausting retries** | `SendError` with the last gateway response attached (`e.response`). | Same behavior. |
| **Migration note** | Default behavior is 3 retries, 250 ms back‑off, 30 s timeout. | Defaults were changed to be more aggressive (5 retries, 500 ms back‑off) and faster‑failing (15 s timeout). If your service relied on the v2 timing, you should set the v2 values explicitly after upgrading. |

### Summary of the differences
- **More retries** in v3 (5 vs. 3) → gives the SDK a better chance to succeed under transient failures.
- **Longer back‑off** in v3 (500 ms vs. 250 ms) → spreads out retry attempts, reducing pressure on a throttled broker.
- **Shorter overall timeout** in v3 (15 s vs. 30 s) → the operation will fail faster if the retries cannot succeed within the tighter budget.
- The underlying retry mechanism (automatic handling of retryable error codes, raising `SendError` after the final attempt) remains the same across both versions.

If you need the exact v2 timing after moving to v3, simply pass the older values (`max_retries=3`, `retry_backoff_ms=250`, `timeout_ms=30000`) when calling `Client.send()`

All official Android development is done through Android Studio, Google's IDE built on JetBrains' IntelliJ platform. It
bundles the Android SDK, an emulator manager, a layout editor, a Compose live preview, profiling tools, and Gradle build
integration into a single application.
Installation Checklist
1
Install the JDK (Android Studio now bundles its own JetBrains Runtime, so a separate JDK install is usually
unnecessary).
2
Download and install Android Studio from developer.android.com.
3
On first launch, use the Setup Wizard to download the latest stable Android SDK Platform and Build-Tools.
4
Create at least one Android Virtual Device (AVD) through the Device Manager to test on a simulated phone, or enable
USB debugging on a physical device.
5
Install the Kotlin plugin (bundled by default in modern releases).
Project Build System: Gradle
Every Android project is built with Gradle, a build automation tool that compiles source code, processes resources,
resolves dependencies from Maven/Google repositories, and packages everything into an installable APK or a
publishable Android App Bundle (AAB). Build configuration is written in Kotlin DSL (build.gradle.kts) or Groovy
(build.gradle).
// app/build.gradle.kts
android {
namespace = "com.example.myapp"
compileSdk = 35
defaultConfig {
applicationId = "com.example.myapp"
minSdk = 24
targetSdk = 35
versionCode = 1
versionName = "1.0"
}
}
dependencies {
implementation("androidx.core:core-ktx:1.13.1")
}
SDK Versions to Know

minSdk — the oldest Android version the app will install on.

targetSdk — the version the app has been tested against and opts into behavior for.

compileSdk — the SDK version used to compile the code; should track the latest stable release.
Emulator vs. physical device
The emulator is convenient for everyday iteration, but always validate performance-sensitive features
(camera, sensors, background limits, real network conditions) on a physical device before release.
CHAPTER 3
Kotlin Programming Essentials
Kotlin is a statically typed, modern language that runs on the JVM (and can also compile to native code or JavaScript). It
was designed to eliminate common Java pitfalls such as null pointer exceptions, while remaining fully interoperable with
existing Java libraries — which is why Google made it the preferred language for Android.

Because onCreateView() and onDestroyView() can run multiple times while the underlying Fragment
instance stays alive, any View reference held past onDestroyView() causes a memory leak. Always null
out view-binding references in onDestroyView().
Fragments vs. Compose Navigation
In a pure Jetpack Compose app, Fragments are often unnecessary — a single Activity hosts a NavHost, and each
'screen' is simply a composable function. Many production apps today are in a hybrid state, hosting Compose content

CHAPTER 7
Building UI with XML Layouts and Views
The classic Android View system describes screens declaratively in XML, then binds that XML to interactive Kotlin/Java
code at runtime. Even in a Compose-first codebase, reading XML layouts remains a core skill because of the volume of
existing production code that still uses it.
ConstraintLayout
ConstraintLayout is the recommended root layout for complex screens because it lets every view's position be defined
relative to other views or to the parent, producing a flat view hierarchy that renders efficiently.


LinearLayout — arranges children in a single row or column.

FrameLayout — stacks children on top of one another; commonly used as a Fragment container.

ScrollView / NestedScrollView — makes a single-child layout vertically scrollable.


View Binding generates a strongly typed binding class for every XML layout, replacing the error-prone findViewById()

CHAPTER 1
Introduction to iOS Development
iOS is Apple's mobile operating system, powering the iPhone and, in closely related forms, the iPad (iPadOS), Apple
Watch (watchOS), Apple TV (tvOS), and Vision Pro (visionOS). iOS development is distinguished by a tightly controlled
hardware/software ecosystem: a small number of device models, a single official distribution channel (the App Store), and
a strong emphasis on consistent design through Apple's Human Interface Guidelines.
How an iOS App Is Put Together
Every iOS app has a single entry point defined by an App struct (in SwiftUI) or an AppDelegate/SceneDelegate pair (in
UIKit). From there, the app presents a hierarchy of screens built from views and view controllers, all managed within an
app lifecycle that iOS itself controls — suspending, backgrounding, or terminating the app as system resources require.
Languages and Frameworks

Swift — Apple's modern, safe, and expressive language, introduced in 2014 and now the standard for all new iOS
development.

Objective-C — the original Apple platform language; still present in older codebases and some system frameworks.

SwiftUI — Apple's modern, declarative UI framework, introduced in 2019.

UIKit — the original, imperative UI framework, still the backbone of most production apps and fully interoperable with
SwiftUI.
The Two UI Toolkits
As with Android, iOS today has two coexisting UI approaches. UIKit is imperative: you create UIView and
UIViewController objects and mutate their properties directly. SwiftUI is declarative: you describe views as a function of
state using structs conforming to the View protocol, and the framework re-renders automatically when that state changes.
Apple's frameworks provide bridges (UIViewRepresentable and UIHostingController) so the two can be mixed freely
within a single app.
Why this matters
Most production iOS codebases were started before 2019 and are therefore built primarily on UIKit, with
SwiftUI adopted incrementally for new screens. A working iOS developer needs fluency in both.
Key Concepts at a Glance

View / View Controller — a single screen or a reusable piece of UI.

Scene — an instance of your app's UI, supporting multiple simultaneous windows on iPad and Mac.

App Delegate — receives app-level lifecycle events (launch, background, termination).

Storyboard / SwiftUI View — the two ways screens can be declared and connected.

Segue / NavigationStack — mechanisms for moving between screens.
CHAPTER 2
Setting Up Xcode and the Development Environment
All official iOS development happens in Xcode, Apple's IDE, which is only available on macOS. Xcode bundles the Swift
compiler, Interface Builder, the iOS Simulator, debugging and profiling tools (Instruments), and integrated support for
version control and App Store submission.

touchscreen mobile devices such as smartphones and tablets, and extended to wearables (Wear OS), televisions
(Android TV), cars (Android Auto), and large screens/foldables. It is the most widely deployed mobile operating system in
the world, which makes Android application development one of the highest-demand skills in software engineering.

An Android application is a collection of loosely coupled components — Activities, Fragments, Services, Broadcast
Receivers, and Content Providers — that the Android framework instantiates and manages on the developer's behalf.
Unlike a traditional desktop program with a single entry point (a main() function), an Android app has no single controlling
entry point. Instead, the operating system decides which component to start based on user interaction, system events, or
requests from other apps, and manages each component's lifecycle independently.

imperative UI) uses XML layout files paired with Java/Kotlin code that manipulates View objects directly. The modern
approach, Jetpack Compose, is a declarative UI toolkit written entirely in Kotlin, where the UI is described as a function
of state and automatically recomposes when that state changes. New projects are generally started in Compose, but
understanding the View system remains essential because most production codebases still contain it.

It is the primary write path of the SDK and is safe to call concurrently from multiple threads on a shared `Client` instance. The call blocks until either the gateway acknowledges the event or the configured timeout elapses, whichever comes first.

## Example

```python
from nimbus import Client

client = Client(api_key="nk_live_...")
response = client.send(
    message="order.created",
    topic="orders",
    retry_backoff_ms=750,
)
```
